## AND
# GOVERNMENT,
->*Considered relatively to each other.*<-

## OBJECT OF THIS WORK.

EVERY Science requires a particular Language, because every Science has ideas that are unique to it. It seems that one should begin by creating this Language: but one begins by speaking & by writing, and the Language remains to be made. This is where economic Science <note>original: "Science économique"; Condillac was a pioneer in arguing that economics should be treated as a rigorous, systematic science like physics or geometry.</note> stands, whose object

<keywords>economic science, linguistic precision, definitions, commerce, government, Condillac</keywords>

( ij )

is that of this Work itself. It is, among other things, that which we propose to provide <note>original: "ſuppléer"; in this context, Condillac means to supply the missing precise language and definitions he mentioned on the previous page.</note>.

This Work has three Parts.

In the first, I provide elementary notions regarding **Commerce**, which I determine based on suppositions <note>Condillac uses "suppositions" to describe what we would now call theoretical models or thought experiments—simplified scenarios used to isolate and understand specific economic principles.</note>; and I develop the principles of **Economic Science**. In the second, I make other suppositions to judge the influence that **Commerce** and **Government** must have on each other. In the third, I consider them both according to the facts, in order to rely on experience <note>original: "l’expérience"; here meaning empirical observation and historical evidence rather than a personal trial.</note> as much as on reasoning.

I will often say very common things. But if it were necessary to observe them to pro- <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("par-") at the end of the page, likely leading to the word "parvenir" or "to reach/attain" in the following text.</note>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the theoretical scenario introduced on the previous page, where an isolated tribe has just completed its first harvest. It examines the psychological and practical definitions of "abundance" based on the community's needs and fears.</meta>

can only subsist on the product of the fields it cultivates.

Suppose further that after having set aside the grain <note>original: "bled"; an archaic spelling of *blé*, meaning wheat or grain</note> necessary for sowing the lands, it has one hundred measures <term>muids: a historical French unit of volume for dry goods, roughly equivalent to 1,800 liters in Paris, though it varied by region</term> left; and that with this quantity, it can wait for a second harvest without fear of running out.

In order that, according to our supposition, this quantity removes all fear of running out, it must be sufficient not only for its needs, but also for its fears. Now, this is something that can only be found in a certain abundance. Indeed, when one judges according to their fears, that which would only suffice in the strictest sense does not suffice; and one believes they find what is sufficient only in that which abounds to a certain degree.

The quantity remaining to our small tribe, once the seeds have been set aside, thus constitutes what is called **abundance** for this year. Consequently, if it has

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of a hypothetical tribe's grain supply, moving from the psychological definition of abundance to the practical difficulties of measuring economic resources and predicting future needs.</meta>

a few more measures <note>original: "muids"</note>, it will be in **overabundance**; and it will be in **scarcity** <note>original: "disette"</note>, if it has a few less.

If a people could judge, with precision, the ratio between the quantity of grain <note>original: "bled"; an archaic spelling of *blé*</note> they possess and the quantity required for their consumption, knowing this ratio would always let them know, with that same precision, whether they are in abundance, overabundance, or scarcity.

But they cannot judge this ratio with precision: for they have no way to ensure exactly either the quantity of grain they have, or the quantity they will consume. They can do so even less because they cannot store it without waste <term>déchet: the natural loss of grain during storage due to pests, rot, or dehydration</term>, and the precise amount of this waste is of such a nature that it cannot be predicted. If they judge it, then, it is only an approximation, and based on the experience of several years.

However, in whatever manner they

<meta>This page completes the sentence from the previous page regarding how a community estimates its grain supply. It moves from the psychological perception of wealth to the physical reality of surplus and the dangers of spoilage.</meta>

judges it, it is always true to say that they believe themselves to be in **abundance**, when they think they have a quantity of grain <note>original: "bled"; an archaic spelling of *blé*</note> sufficient to remove any fear of running out; that they believe themselves to be in **overabundance**, when they think they have a quantity more than sufficient to meet all their fears; and that they believe themselves to be in **scarcity** <note>original: "disette"</note>, when they think they have only a quantity that does not suffice to dispel them.

It is therefore in the *opinion* <note>In this context, "opinion" refers to the collective perception or subjective estimation of the community</note> one has of quantities, rather than in the quantities themselves, that abundance, overabundance, or scarcity are found: but they are only found in opinion because they are assumed to be present in the actual quantities.

<margin>Useless overabundance and useful overabundance.</margin>

Several consecutive years of a large harvest would thus only burden the Tribe <note>original: "Peuplade"; referring to a small community or settled population</note> with a useless overabundance, and it would soon happen that they would sow less land.

But harvests that do not suffice for the needs of the Tribe will make felt the necessity of preserving grain <note>original: "bled"; an archaic spelling of *blé*</note> when there is a surplus. They will therefore seek the means to do so, and when they have found them, the grain that was useless in years of overabundance will become useful in years of scarcity <note>original: "disette"</note>. The hundred measures <note>original: "muids"; an ancient French unit of volume for dry goods, which varied by region but often represented a large quantity</note> that the Tribe has not consumed, and which it has known how to preserve, will supplement what it lacks during several years when there remains for its consumption—after the <term>seeds have been set aside</term> <note>original: "semences prélevées"; the portion of the harvest reserved for the next planting rather than for immediate food</note>—only sixty or eighty measures.

Now, since the value of things is founded on need, it is natural that a more keenly felt need gives things a greater value, and that a less keenly felt need gives them a lesser one. The value of things therefore increases in scarcity and decreases in abundance.

In abundance, value can even decrease to the point of becoming null. A **surplus** <note>original: "surabondant"; referring to an excess of goods beyond what is currently required.</note>, for example, will be without value whenever no use can be made of it, since it will then be completely useless.

But if it is considered in relation to subsequent years, when the harvest might not be sufficient, it will have a value, because one judges that it could become part of the quantity necessary for the needs one will then have.

In this case, I estimate that my grain is worth to you what your wine is worth to me, and you estimate that your wine is worth to me what my grain is worth to you.

But if my surplus suffices for your consumption, and yours does not suffice for mine, I will not give mine in its entirety for yours: for what I would yield to you would be worth more to you than what you would yield to me would be worth to me.

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the Variation of Prices.*

<margin>The price of things varies.</margin>
We have just seen that price is founded upon value. Now, as value varies, price must also vary. There are several causes for this variation.

<margin>1st. In proportion to abundance and scarcity.</margin>
First, it is evident that abundance and scarcity cause price to vary, just as they do value, and they cause it to vary in proportion to the greater or lesser <term>need</term> <note>original: "beſoin." In this context, it refers to both a biological necessity and the subjective desire for an object, which modern economists would call "demand."</note>.

If we were to suppose the surplus grain was distributed among the granaries of twelve people, and on the contrary, all the surplus wine was kept in the cellars of a single person, then the price would no longer be the same as in the first supposition: for the price of the grain would fall, and that of the wine would rise.

When several people have a need to exchange a commodity, this competition therefore causes its price to fall; and the lack of competition causes the price of the commodity they wish to have delivered to rise. Now, as competition is greater, lesser, or non-existent, sometimes on one side and sometimes on the other, it happens that prices rise and fall alternately.

## How *Commerce* increases the mass of wealth?

<margin>The land is the sole source of wealth.</margin>

<margin>Why we are inclined to think the opposite.</margin>
The mistake commonly made on this subject stems from the fact that we speak of goods in **commerce** <note>In this context, "commerce" refers to the general exchange and trade of goods in a marketplace.</note> as if they possessed an **absolute value**; consequently, we judge that justice requires those who engage in **exchanges** to mutually give equal value for equal value. Far from noticing that two **contracting parties** each give the other "less" for "more," we think, without much reflection, that this cannot be the case; it seems that for one to always give less, the other would have to be enough of a dupe to always give more—an assumption that cannot be made.

<margin>Through exchange, what was not wealth becomes wealth.</margin>
We are not expected to put up for sale the things necessary for our own **consumption**; rather, it is our **surplus** <note>Original: "surabondant." This refers to the excess production or goods that exceed a person's immediate personal needs.</note>, as I have noted several times. We want to surrender something that is **useless** to us to procure something that is **necessary**: we want to give less for more.

<summary>The author argues that the idea of "equal value for equal value" in trade is a fallacy caused by viewing value as absolute; instead, trade occurs because both parties exchange a useless surplus for a necessary good, thus both receiving more than they give.</summary>

The **surplus** <note>Original: "surabondant." As noted previously, this refers to the excess production beyond what the producer needs for their own survival.</note> of the **farmers** <note>Original: "Colons." In the economic language of the 18th century, this term refers to those who cultivate the land, such as settlers or tenant farmers.</note> is what provides the entire foundation for **trade**. This surplus is wealth so long as they can find a way to exchange it; this is because they procure something that has value to them, while delivering something that has value to others.

If they were unable to make exchanges, their surplus would remain with them and would have no value to them. In fact, surplus **grain** <note>Original: "bled," a historical spelling of "blé" (wheat or grain).</note> that I keep in my granaries without being able to exchange it is no more wealth to me than the grain I have not yet pulled from the earth. Consequently, I will sow less next year, and despite having a smaller harvest, I will be no poorer for it.

<margin>Merchants therefore increase the mass of wealth.</margin>
Now, **merchants** are the channels of communication through which the surplus flows. From places where it has no value, it passes to places where it acquires value; and wherever it is deposited, it becomes wealth.

<summary>The author explains that surplus production only constitutes wealth when it can be exchanged, as unused goods have no inherent value to the producer. The **Merchant** <note>Original: "Commerçant."</note> thus makes, in a sense, something out of nothing. He does not till the soil himself, but he causes it to be tilled. A spring that vanishes into rocks and sand is not a form of wealth for me; but it becomes one if I build an **aqueduct** to guide it into my meadows. This spring represents the surplus production that we owe to the Farmers, and the aqueduct represents the Merchants.

# CHAPTER VII.

## *How needs, by multiplying, give birth to the Arts, and how the Arts increase the mass of wealth?*

<margin>Things of primary necessity, and things of secondary necessity.</margin>
Just as I have distinguished between **natural needs** and **artificial needs** <note>Original: *besoins factices*. These are "artificial" in the sense that they are acquired through social habit or luxury rather than biological requirement.</note>, I shall also distinguish between two kinds of necessary things: those of **primary necessity**, which I relate to natural needs; and those of **secondary necessity**, which I relate to artificial needs.

Fruits, such as the earth produces by its own fertility alone, are of primary necessity for a **Savage** <note>In 18th-century philosophy, the "Savage" (*Sauvage*) was a hypothetical or idealized figure used to represent humanity in its most basic "state of nature," before the complexities of modern civilization and commerce.</note>, because they are necessary to him as a consequence of his physical constitution; and our wines and our brandies <note>Original: *eaux-de-vie*.</note> would be of secondary necessity for him if, by trading with us, he formed a habit of these drinks.

Now, not only must he be reimbursed for all his advances <note>As established on the previous page, "advances" refers to the merchant's upfront capital investments, such as the purchase price of goods and transportation costs.</note>, he must also find a profit in conducting his trade.

This profit is exactly what is called *wages* <note>original: *salaire*. In modern English, we distinguish between a laborer's "wage" and a merchant's "profit," but in 18th-century economic thought, the merchant's profit was often viewed as the "wage" or "salary" they earned for their labor, skill, and risk.</note>. We understand that it must be earned and distributed successively across all the goods he sells; and that it must be sufficient for his subsistence—that is to say, to provide him with the use of things of first necessity <note>Essential items required for survival, such as basic food and shelter.</note> and second necessity <note>Often referred to as "comforts," these are items that are not strictly essential for life but are considered necessary for a decent standard of living according to one's social standing.</note>.

But to what extent should Merchants enjoy these things? This is something that will regulate itself, depending on how competition <note>original: *concurrence*. This refers to the market force where multiple sellers vie for buyers, naturally driving prices and profits toward a baseline.</note> forces them to live with more or less economy; and as this competition will dictate the law to everyone equally, we will know, according to general custom, the level of comfort to which each of them is entitled to aspire. The value of the form <note>original: *valeur de la forme*. In this context, it refers to the added value provided by the craftsman's labor as they transform raw materials into a finished product.</note> can only be the value of the labor that provides it. It is the wage owed to the Worker <note>original: *Ouvrier*. Referring here to a laborer, artisan, or craftsman who adds value to raw materials.</note>.

If one were to pay this wage with productions <note>original: *productions*. This refers to raw agricultural goods or resources harvested directly from the land.</note>, one would give the Worker as much as they have a right to consume throughout the time their labor lasts.

When the work is done, the value of the form is therefore equivalent to the value of the productions the Worker is assumed to have consumed.

These productions are no more. But <margin>Landed wealth replaces itself; movable wealth accumulates.</margin> if one considers that they have been replaced by others, one will judge that the quantity of landed wealth <note>original: *richeffes foncieres*. Raw goods and produce from the earth.</note> remains the same, on average years <note>original: *années communes*. A period of time representing a typical harvest cycle or standard year.</note>.

Landed wealth is only replaced insofar as it is destroyed. Produced in order to be consumed, it is only reproduced in proportion to consumption; and the quantity consumed is determined by need—a need that has limits.

<summary>This page defines the value of craftsmanship as being equal to the cost of the worker's consumption during the production process. It highlights the cycle of landed wealth, which must be consumed to be reproduced, versus movable wealth, which accumulates over time.</summary>

# CHAPTER X.

### *By what labors wealth is produced, distributed, and preserved.*

<margin>How the Farmer and the Artisan enrich themselves through their labors</margin>
We have just seen two kinds of labor. Some give rise to productions <note>original: *productions*; here referring specifically to the raw outputs of nature and agriculture</note>; others give raw materials the forms that make them suitable for various uses, and which, for this reason, have a value.

If the Farmer <term>Farmer: *Colon*; a cultivator of the land, emphasizing the role of one who settles and works the soil</term> works with intelligence and assiduity, he multiplies his productions and improves their species <note>meaning he improves the varieties of crops or livestock breeds</note>.

If the Artisan <term>Artisan: *Artisan*; a skilled craftsman who transforms raw materials into finished goods</term> works with the same intelligence and the same assiduity <note>original: *assiduité*; meaning steady, diligent, and persistent effort</note>, he multiplies his works, and he gives more value to the forms he makes the raw materials <term>raw materials: *matieres premieres*; the basic substances provided by nature, such as wool, wood, or ore, before they are processed</term> take.

The Farmer <term>Farmer: *Colon*; specifically a cultivator or settler who works the land to produce food and fiber</term> and the Artisan thus enrich themselves in proportion as they work more, and as they work better.

The Farmer enriches himself because he produces more than he can consume.

The Artisan enriches himself because, by giving forms to raw materials, he produces values equivalent to all the consumption he can make <note>The author argues that the artisan's labor creates enough value to "repay" or cover the cost of all the food and goods he needs to survive, thereby adding to the total stock of wealth</note>.

It will no doubt be said that the Farmer and the Artisan have charges <term>charges: *charges*; the various financial burdens, fees, or social obligations imposed upon a worker</term> to pay, and I agree that these charges could often reduce them to misery. But, to simplify, I suppose them exempt from all taxes <note>original: *impôt*</note>. We shall treat elsewhere of the subsidies <term>subsidies: *subsides*; in this period, the term refers to the tax revenues or financial grants provided by the people to the State</term> owed to the State.

<margin>How they are rich relative to their condition.</margin>
Not all labors are equally easy.

In the easiest tasks <term>easiest tasks: *les plus faciles*; refers to unskilled labor that requires little training or specialized knowledge</term>, there are more competitors <term>competitors: *concurrens*; other workers seeking the same job</term>, and one is reduced to lower wages. Consequently, one consumes less, or even consumes only what is absolutely necessary. If these necessities were never lacking, one would be rich relative to one's condition <note>original: *riche par rapport à son état*; the author suggests that "wealth" is relative; a worker is "rich" if their basic needs are reliably met according to their social standing</note>. But how can one ensure this, if one does not earn anything beyond that? If, during working days, one consumes their entire wage, how will one survive during the days when one does not work? <note>This highlights the precariousness of the working class, who face periods of non-earning due to illness, seasonal fluctuations, or religious holidays</note>

In more difficult tasks, there are fewer competitors, and one obtains higher wages. One will therefore be able to consume more. One will be better fed, better clothed, and better housed. If one then wishes to save <term>save: *économiser*; to practice thrift by withholding a portion of one's earnings from immediate consumption</term>, or cut back on one's consumption, one will have a surplus <note>original: *au-delà*; literally "beyond," meaning a reserve of value</note>, and one will be rich in the true sense of the word.

When one writes, one is continually stopped, and precisely by the words that are in everyone's mouth <note>The author is reflecting on the difficulty of economic theory: the most common words—like wealth, value, or necessity—are often the hardest to define precisely because they are used so casually in daily life</note>...

Their consumption—at once greater and more varied—will increasingly stimulate **industry** <note>In this period, "industry" refers generally to diligent labor and manufacturing rather than heavy factories</note>; and, consequently, **Agriculture**, the **Arts**, and **Commerce** will flourish all the more, as the new needs people have created for themselves will offer new profits to the **Tiller** <note>original: *Laboureur*; specifically a farmer who owns a plow and team</note>, the **Artisan**, and the **Merchant**.

<margin>The proportion established between production and consumption.</margin>
During this revolution, production and consumption will continually balance one another; and, according to the proportion between them, they will cause prices to rise and fall—

<summary>This page describes an economic feedback loop where urban demand encourages farmers to eliminate fallow land, thereby increasing production, raising land values for owners, and fueling the growth of trade and industry.</summary>

—in turn, the price of each thing.
If consumption <note>meaning demand</note> is greater, everything will become more expensive: if, on the contrary, it is production <note>meaning supply</note> that is greater, everything will be cheaper. But these variations will have few disadvantages; for the complete freedom enjoyed by **Trade** <note>original: *Commerce*</note> will soon proportion production to consumption, and will set each thing at the price it ought to have. Such is the first foundation of the right of property.

At harvest time, everyone could say once more: *if this uncultivated field was mine because it fell to me as my share, now that it is cultivated, it is mine by more than one title, since its cultivation is my own work. It is mine with all its produce, because its produce is at the same time the product of my labor.*

Property in land is therefore founded at once upon the **division** <note>original: *partage*; the act of partitioning or sharing out the land among the settlers</note> that was made of it, and upon the labor that makes it fertile.

When, in the course of time, some **Colonists** <note>original: *Colons*; settlers or farmers</note> had acquired more land than they could cultivate by themselves, they were no less justified in regarding all these lands as their own. Their ownership of them was secured by the **transfer** <note>original: *cession*; the act of legally surrendering or giving up a right or property to another</note> from those to whom the lands had previously belonged. ### All these properties are sacred.

One could not, without injustice, deprive the **Manufacturer** of his profit, nor the **Worker** of his wage. One could not, therefore, force the **Colonist** <term>Colonist: original *Colon*, here referring to a landowner or agricultural entrepreneur</term> to sell his grain below its value, just as one could not force those who need it to pay more than it is worth. These truths are so simple that they may perhaps go unnoticed, and one might even be surprised that I have noted them. It will, however, be necessary to remember them.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### Of Metals Considered as Merchandise.

<margin>Why gold, silver, and copper are the first metals that men knew.</margin>
GOLD, silver, and copper are the first metals that men knew. They were often found on the surface of the earth without even having been sought. Rains, floods, and a thousand accidents uncovered them; many rivers carry them <note>The author refers to "alluvial" deposits, where metal particles or nuggets are naturally washed down from mountains into riverbeds, making them accessible without deep mining.</note>.

Moreover, these metals are recognized quite easily when they are pure and unmixed, or when their purity is at least little altered. This is what always happens with gold, often with silver, and quite frequently with copper, though more rarely <note>In chemistry, gold is a "noble" metal because it does not oxidize or rust; the author observes that these metals are often found in their "native" state, looking like metal even in nature.</note>. Nature offers them provided with all their properties.

## C H A P T E R XIV.
### Of Metals considered as Money.

<margin>At the origin of societies, peoples had no measures.</margin>
WHEN, in the previous chapters, I assumed the existence of measures, it was solely to speak with more precision regarding the respective value of the things being exchanged. It appears that at the origin of societies, peoples had none; even today, several still do not have them. This is because we are content to judge the quantity of things by eye whenever we have no interest in looking at them closely.

However, when I deliver to you a quantity of grain <note>original: "bled," an archaic spelling of *blé* (wheat or grain).</note>, valued at ten ounces of silver, to receive from you a quantity of wine of the same price, it is not certain that this exchange is equally advantageous for you and for me, even though these two quantities appear to be the equivalent of one another.

Indeed, if the grain I have delivered to you is absolutely necessary to me, and the wine you have given me is surplus <note>original: "surabondant," referring to an excess of goods beyond what is required for one's own consumption or survival.</note> for you, the advantage will be on your side, and the disadvantage on mine.

# CHAPTER XVI.
## *On the Circulation of Money.*

<margin>What is meant by the circulation of money.</margin>
Every year, at the appointed times, the Farmers bring to the Cities the full price of their leases <note>original: "baux"; the rent or contractual payments made by a tenant farmer to a landowner for the use of their land.</note>: every market day, they sell some commodities, and, consequently, they carry back, in small amounts <note>original: "en détail"; literally "in detail," meaning piece-meal or through many small transactions rather than a single lump sum.</note>, to their Village the sums they had paid to the Landowners.

The Merchant, in the course of the year, receives in small amounts the price of the Goods he purchased in bulk <term>bulk: "en gros," referring to the purchase of large quantities of goods at once, typically for a lower unit price</term>; and the Craftsman, who purchased raw materials in bulk, resells them in small portions once he has worked them. Thus, daily sales reimburse, through small sums, the large sums

Money is therefore distributed continually, only to be gathered afterwards as if in reservoirs, from which it spreads through a multitude of small channels, which carry it back to the primary reservoirs; from where it spreads again, and where it returns once more. This continual movement, which gathers money to distribute it, and distributes it to gather it, is what we call *circulation.*

I agree that the Merchant and the Artisan can buy on credit, to pay later at various intervals. <margin>Credit takes the place of money.</margin>

It would be advantageous for the use of credit to be established, because then a Merchant and an Artisan could, without ready money, have a stock—the former of goods, the latter of raw materials; and consequently, a greater number of industrious men would contribute to the progress of Commerce. For this to happen, good faith must bring about confidence. This is what happens above all in Republics that have strong morals <term>morals: original "mœurs," a term used by Enlightenment thinkers to describe the shared customs, ethics, and habits of a society</term>, that is to say, simplicity and frugality.

<meta>This page transitions from discussing the necessity of credit for urban trades (Merchants and Artisans) to the unique economic structure of the rural agricultural sector, where physical currency is less essential due to in-kind payments.</meta>

<margin>Farmers can cover almost all the costs of cultivation without money.</margin>
The Merchant and the Artisan can do nothing without money, or at least without credit. It is not the same for Farmers. While one or the other <note>referring to money or credit discussed on the previous page</note> is necessary for them for the items they must buy in the City, they do not have the same need for them to provide for the costs of cultivation. This is because they can pay all the Rural Inhabitants <term>Rural Inhabitants: original "Habitans de la Campagne," referring to the local laborers, peasants, and village craftsmen</term> who work for them with the grain they harvest, with the drinks they produce, and with the livestock they raise. Custom <note>original: "l'usage," referring to the established social traditions that governed rural life</note> regulates the wages they owe, and the goods they deliver in payment are valued according to the current Market price.

<margin>This is why money circulates little in the countryside.</margin>
Thus, no money is spent in the Countryside, or very little is spent; and since one can only earn money on one side in proportion to how much is spent on the other, it follows that those who work for the Farmers earn little money, or earn none at all. Money, therefore, circulates less in the Countryside than elsewhere.

<margin>Reciprocal debts between Cities regulate all exchange operations.</margin>

<margin>Reciprocal debts are either equal or unequal.</margin>

Debts can also be unequal: Lyon might owe Paris three hundred thousand francs, and Paris might owe Lyon four hundred thousand.

<margin>When debts are equal, the exchange is at par, and is conducted as an equal sum for an equal sum, but not as an equal value for an equal value.</margin>
In the case of equal debts on both sides, if we consider only this factor, it is certain that two Merchants—one in Paris who needs one hundred thousand francs in Lyon, and another in Lyon who needs one hundred thousand francs in Paris—should make this exchange as an equal sum for an equal sum. For they both find the same advantage in giving one hundred thousand francs for one hundred thousand francs; and since this exchange does not require one to pay more costs than the other, neither is entitled to demand more than one hundred thousand francs.

## CHAPTER XIX.
### *On the comparative value of the Metals from which Money is made.*

<margin>
Metals are rare or abundant according to their greater or lesser quantity, and according to whether they are put to more or fewer uses.
</margin>
Copper, silver, and gold, which are used in coinage, have—like all commodities—a value based on their **utility**; and this value increases or decreases in proportion to whether they are judged more rare or more abundant.

<summary>The author concludes that the state should regulate loans to prevent abuse while supporting small-scale merchants, then begins a new chapter explaining that the value of gold, silver, and copper is determined by their utility and scarcity.</summary>
<keywords>clandestine loans, Entrepreneurs, Commercial Hubs, monetary value, utility, scarcity, gold, silver, copper</keywords>

--- Page 213 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 196 regarding the intrinsic and comparative value of precious metals, specifically moving from the concept of utility to a mathematical demonstration of how scarcity dictates the exchange rates between copper, silver, and gold.</meta>

( 197 )

Let us suppose that there is one hundred times as much copper as silver in Europe, and twenty times as much silver as gold. In this hypothetical case, where we consider these metals only in relation to their quantity, it would require one hundred pounds of copper to create a value equivalent to one pound of silver, and twenty pounds of silver to create a value equivalent to one pound of gold. We would express these ratios by saying that copper is to silver as one hundred to one, and that silver is to gold as twenty to one.

But if very abundant mines of silver, and especially of gold, were to be discovered, these metals would no longer hold the same **relative value** <note>The "relative value" refers to the worth of one metal when compared to another; this ratio fluctuates based on supply and demand rather than remaining a fixed, permanent number.</note>. For example, copper might then be to silver as fifty to one, and silver would be to gold as ten to one.

There cannot always be the same quantity of each of these metals within **Commerce** <note>In this 18th-century context, "Commerce" refers to the broad system of trade, the market, and the circulation of money in the economy.</note>. Their relative value must therefore vary from time to time.

However, this value does not vary based on quantity alone; because even if the quantity remains the same, there is another cause that can make these metals rarer or more abundant.

We shall apply the same reasoning to gold and silver. Suppose that while these metals are at a ratio <term>ratio: "rapport" — the exchange rate or proportional value between two currencies or metals.</term> of twenty to one, a custom is introduced of lavishly using silver on furniture and clothing; silver will become scarcer, and might then stand in a ratio of ten to one with gold. Metals are therefore scarcer or more abundant depending on whether we put them to more or fewer uses. Consequently, we can only judge their **relative value**, insofar as we can compare the uses made of one with those made of the other.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of three hypothetical provinces—one in scarcity, one in surplus, and one self-sufficient—explaining how their isolated markets prevent a unified price for grain until trade is permitted.</meta>

( 210 )

Each province values the <term>grain</term> <note>original: "bled." While literally meaning corn or grain, in 18th-century France, it almost exclusively referred to wheat, the vital staple of the diet and economy.</note> according to the ratio it perceives, or believes it perceives, between the quantity and the need. If it judges that the quantity is not sufficient, the price is high; if it judges it sufficient, the price is low.

I call <term>proportional prices</term> <note>These are prices that correctly reflect the local relationship between supply (quantity) and demand (need).</note> those that are established upon such ratios. From this we see that, whatever the prices may be, they are always proportional, because they are always founded on the opinion held regarding quantity relative to need. However, the price that is current in one of our provinces, though proportional within its own borders, would be disproportional for the others, and cannot suit them.

<margin>The same price will only be the true one for all three when they trade with each other with full and complete liberty.</margin>

The prices of grain are only so different in these three provinces because we have forbidden all commerce between them. They will, therefore, no longer be different if we grant them the liberty to reciprocally export from one to another.

<margin>Liberty of trade alone can prevent monopoly.</margin>

<margin>It is in the interest of all that there be the greatest number of Merchants in every branch of trade.</margin>
Every **seller** wants to gain, and to gain as much as he can. There is not one among them who would not wish to drive away all his **competitors** and sell alone, if he were able.

Every **buyer** would like to buy at the lowest **price**, and he would desire that the **sellers**, in competition with one another, offer him goods at a discount.

## *On the Circulation of Grain.* <note>original: "Bleds." In the 18th century, this term was used generally for all types of cereal grains used for bread, though it specifically means wheat.</note>

<margin>Two kinds of scarcity.</margin>
WHEN, not having enough to wait for a second harvest, one has grain, for example, for only nine months, one is threatened with running out if more does not arrive; and the price increases all the more as there is less hope of seeing any arrive.

This price increase, which causes it to rise above the **true price** <note>original: "vrai prix." This is the natural market value where supply and demand balance out.</note>, becomes **dearness** <note>original: "cherté." A technical term in early economics referring to a price spike that makes essential goods unaffordable for the common people.</note>. People then cry out "scarcity," not because there is a total lack of grain, but because there is a threat of running out, and because those who cannot pay for it at its current price are already going without.

This real scarcity, if indeed there is not enough grain, is only a **scarcity of opinion** <note>original: "disette d'opinion." This refers to an artificial shortage caused by fear, panic, or hoarding rather than a physical lack of food.</note> when the grain—which is not lacking in the granaries—is only lacking in the Markets. The circulation of money <note>original: "l'argent" — meaning both silver and currency in general</note> slows down from countryside to countryside, in proportion to how far they are from the principal Cities; and assuming the distance is the same, it slows down further because of the obstacles that make the transport of goods more expensive. As soon as money circulates less, it is rarer; as soon as it is rarer, it has more value; as soon as it has more value, one gives a smaller amount of it for the things one buys; and, consequently, these things appear to be at a lower price than they truly are.

A commodity would always have a fixed value if, being always equally necessary, it existed in the same quantity relative to need across all eras and in all places. It would then be a measure with which we could evaluate the value of money in every century and every location. Wheat <note>original: "bled" — a term used for cereal grains, primarily wheat, which was the staple of the European diet and the basis of the economy</note> is this commodity.

<margin>
It would be advantageous if the price of leases were paid in commodities.

In the common practice of leasing <note>original: "affermer" — the act of a landowner letting out land to a tenant farmer</note> land for money, there is an injury <note>original: "léſion" — an economic disadvantage or loss resulting from a change in market conditions</note> for the Farmer if the grain <note>original: "bled"</note> price falls; and if it rises to a high price, there is an injury to the Landowners. This practice is all the more harmful because the Farmers, all being obliged to pay at the same deadlines and, consequently, to put their harvest up for sale all at once, cause the price of grain to drop every year during the same months—to their great detriment and to the advantage of monopolists. It would therefore be advantageous for the Landowners, for the Farmers, and for the State, if the price of Leases were paid in commodities <note>original: "denrées" — specifically referring here to payment "in kind," or using the actual produce of the land instead of currency</note>. There would be an advantage not only when the grain trade is restricted; there would be an advantage even when it is free, because it would become even freer: for Farmers would no longer be forced to sell at one time rather than another.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the limits of agricultural production introduced in Chapter XXV. It explores the concept of a "maximum capacity" for land and the trade-offs required once that capacity is reached.</meta>

->( 269 )<-

<margin>Productions brought to their final limit of abundance.</margin>
If we suppose that all the lands are under cultivation <note>original: "en valeur" — referring to land that has been improved and made productive</note>, and that each produces as much as it can produce, productions will be at the final limit of abundance, and it will no longer be possible to increase them.

<margin>At that point, productions cannot become more abundant in one category without becoming scarcer in another.</margin>
Then, if we wish to have a greater abundance in one kind of commodity, we must necessarily resolve to have a lesser amount in another kind. To have more fodder, for example, it will be necessary to convert fields that were traditionally sown into meadows; one will therefore have a smaller harvest of wheat <note>original: "bled" — a general term for grain, usually wheat, which was the staple of the French diet</note>.

<margin>The population is greater or smaller depending on the use of the land, and according to how much each man consumes.</margin>
The same productions are not equally suited to the subsistence of animals of all species. Consequently, if the lands are used to feed many horses, they will not be able to feed the same number of men.

Depending on the use of the land, the population will therefore be larger or smaller.

<margin>Simple living lies between two extremes.</margin>
Between a coarse life and a soft life, I would like to distinguish a simple life, and to define its concept, if possible, with some precision.

I envision a coarse life <note>original: "vie grossiere," describing a primitive, unrefined, or rough existence</note> as the initial state our community <note>original: "Peuplade," a term for a small colony or primitive settlement</note> was in; I envision a soft life <note>original: "vie molle," a life of decadent luxury and physical ease</note> in those times when excesses of every kind have corrupted the social morals <note>original: "mœurs," referring to the customs, values, and ethical character of a society</note>. These extremes are easy to grasp. It is between the one and the other that we must find the simple life. But where does it begin, and where does it end? This is something that can only be shown approximately.

<margin>After the founding of Cities, life continued to be simple as long as there were few laws and Agriculture was held in high regard.</margin>
After the founding of Cities, Government could no longer be so simple, and disorders began. The Landowners <term>Propriétaires: specifically those who held title to land, representing the emerging wealthy class</term>, as the wealthiest members of society, found themselves in possession of the primary authority. They seemed to have a greater right to it because, as masters of the land, they had a greater stake <note>original: "intérêt," implying both a financial investment and a personal concern</note> in the general welfare.

<margin>*The employment of Men in a society whose customs are simple.*</margin>

This is the goal toward which the Arts should strive, and where they ought to stop.

## CHAPTER XXVII.

### On Luxury.

<margin>The confused idea that people form of luxury.</margin>
Ever since people began writing about luxury, some have offered its defense <note>original: "apologie"; in the 18th century, an "apology" referred to a formal justification or argument in favor of a concept</note>, while others have written satires against it, and yet nothing is proven. This is because we do not seek to reach a common understanding.

We speak of luxury as if it were something of which we had formed an absolute idea, and yet we have only a relative idea of it. What constitutes luxury for one People is not luxury for another; and for the same People, what once was considered luxury can cease to be so.

Luxury, in the primary sense <note>original: "acception"; the specific meaning or definition of a word as it is understood in context</note> of the term, is the same thing as excess; and when it is used in this sense, we begin to understand each other. But when we forget this primary sense—

<vocab>luxury, defense, satire, absolute idea, relative idea, excess</vocab>

He suggests that luxury should fundamentally be understood as a form of "excess" that varies across different cultures and eras.</summary>
<keywords>luxury, simplicity, excess, economic relativity, social definitions, 18th-century philosophy</keywords>

<margin>What is excess in the eyes of a Savage is not so in the eyes of a Citizen.</margin>
The coarse life of our Tribe <note>original: "Peuplade"; the author uses this term to refer to a hypothetical early society or colony used as a model for economic development</note>, at the time of its establishment, would be an excess of refinements <note>original: "recherches"; in this context, it refers to the elaborate efforts or specialized methods used to satisfy needs</note> in the eyes of a Savage, who, accustomed to living by hunting and fishing, does not understand the necessity of the needs that the Tribe has created for itself. Because the earth, without being worked, provides for his subsistence, it seems to him that those who cultivate it are too refined in their means of subsisting.

There, then, in his judgment, is an excess, which is not one in the judgment of our Tribe, nor in our own.

<margin>Why</margin>
Men judge differently what all agree to call excess, only because, not having the same needs, it is natural that what appears as excess to one does not appear so to another. This is undoubtedly why we have so much trouble knowing what we mean to say when we speak of luxury.

<margin>Luxury consists of things that all Citizens must agree to regard as an excess.</margin>
I distinguish two kinds of excess: those that are so only because they appear as such in the eyes of a certain number of people; and others that are so because they must appear as such in the eyes of everyone. It is in these latter that I place the definition of luxury. Let us see then what things must appear as an excess in the eyes of all.

To judge the disadvantages of luxury in relation to individuals, I distinguish three types: luxury of magnificence, luxury of conveniences, and luxury of frivolities.

<margin>Luxury of magnificence.</margin>

Commerce needs a Power that protects it. I call the revenues granted to this Power *public revenues* or *State revenues*. The question is to know why and by whom they must be paid.

<margin>Every Citizen must make themselves useful.</margin>
A civil society is founded on a contract, express or tacit, by which all Citizens engage themselves, each for their part, to contribute to the common advantage.

In general, to contribute to this advantage, it suffices to be useful; and one will be so, every time they have a profession <note>original: "un état"; in this historical context, this refers to one's station in life, trade, or social standing.</note> and fulfill its duties.

This manner of contributing is an obligation that all Citizens, without exception, contracted by uniting as a body of society.

A useless man is therefore not a Citizen. Being a burden to society, he does nothing for it: it owes him nothing.

<margin>Subsidies or Taxes to be paid.</margin>
But it is not always enough to have a profession and fulfill its duties. In the government of every society

<margin>The owners can pay the subsidies.</margin>

Either the Country inhabited by a Nation provides abundantly everything necessary for the needs of the Citizens; or it provides only a portion, no matter how much care is given to the cultivation of the land.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

### *Of the Respective Wealth of Nations.*

<margin>That there can be only two kinds of wealth.</margin>
**W**e have distinguished between <term>landed wealth: wealth derived from the soil and its natural products (French: 'richesses foncières')</term> and <term>movable wealth: assets that can be moved, such as manufactured goods (French: 'richesses mobiliaires')</term>. Among landed wealth, I include not only all produce, but also all livestock; indeed, they must be regarded as a product of the lands that nourish them.

Among movable wealth, I include all things to which <term>labor: the physical effort applied to raw materials (French: 'main-d'œuvre')</term> has given a new form. This is what all wealth is reduced to; it would be impossible to imagine a third kind.

If one were to say that gold and silver are of another category, I would ask if these metals are not formed in the earth, and if it is not true that they are only truly produced for us when we extract them from the mine and refine them <note>The author is arguing that even precious metals fit into his two-part system: they are "landed" when in the ground and "movable" once processed by human hands.</note>.

<vocab>landed wealth, movable wealth, produce, livestock, labor, metals, gold, silver, mine</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the two fundamental types of wealth in an economy: landed wealth (natural products and livestock) and movable wealth (manufactured goods). The author argues that even precious metals like gold and silver do not constitute a third category, as they originate from the earth and are refined by labor.</summary>
<keywords>wealth classification, landed wealth, movable wealth, Physiocracy, labor, natural resources, livestock, gold and silver</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 325 regarding the classification of wealth. Having established that even precious metals originate from the earth, the author now explains how labor transforms these natural resources into functional "movable wealth" and the role of commerce in establishing their value.</meta>

->( 326 )<-

Gold and silver are therefore <term>landed wealth: assets derived directly from the earth's resources (French: 'richesses foncières')</term>, which, like <term>grain: the primary example of agricultural produce, often spelled 'bled' in 18th-century French</term>, are the product of the earth and of our labor; and these metals become <term>movable wealth: assets that have been manufactured or processed into useful goods (French: 'richesses mobiliaires')</term> once we have caused them to take on forms that make them suitable for various uses—when we have turned them into money, vases, and so forth.

<margin>
Since all wealth is due to labor, the wealthiest nation is the one where people work the most.
</margin>

We have seen that all this wealth only increases in proportion to our labor. We owe all production to the work of the <term>Farmer: considered by thinkers of this era to be the "primary" producer (French: 'Cultivateur')</term>; and we owe to the labor of the Craftsman or the Artist all the forms given to raw materials.

We have also seen that all this wealth only achieves its true value insofar as <term>circulation: the flow of goods and money through an economy (French: 'circulation')</term> moves it from places where it is in surplus to places where it is needed. This circulation is the result of Commerce. The value of wealth is therefore partly due to the labor of Merchants.

<summary>The author explains that gold and silver transition from "landed wealth" to "movable wealth" through human labor and manufacturing. He concludes that labor—whether from farmers, craftsmen, or merchants—is the fundamental driver of national wealth and value.</summary>

The labors of this power thus contribute to the growth, as well as the preservation, of wealth.

Based on this summary, it is easy to judge which Nation ought to be the wealthiest.

It is the one where there is, at once, the greatest amount of labor of every kind.

In England, exportation is rarely prohibited; but the freedom to import is more or less restricted by duties <note>original: "droits," referring to customs duties or tariffs</note> which rise or fall according to circumstances.

It is evident that, if she could likewise trade in all of Europe, she would sell with even greater advantage, since a larger number of buyers would make a greater number of demands. If her advantage is not as great as it could be, it is simply because she cannot trade everywhere with equal ease.

Some will no doubt argue that the price of grain will rise <note>original: "renchériront," meaning to become more expensive or increase in cost</note> in France if we sell it to every foreigner who requests it.

## CHAPTER XXX.

### *A Brief Recapitulation of the First Part.*

The value of things—or the esteem in which we hold them—is based on their utility <term>utility: in 18th-century economic thought, this refers to the capacity of a good to satisfy a specific human want or need</term> and is in proportion to our needs. From this, it follows that a surplus <note>original: "le ſurabondant," referring to quantities of goods that exceed current requirements</note>, when considered strictly as a surplus, possesses no value; it can only acquire value insofar as one judges that it will eventually become necessary.

Our needs are either natural or artificial <note>original: "factices," meaning needs created by social custom, luxury, or habit rather than biological survival</note>.

In the isolated man <note>a common Enlightenment trope referring to man in a "state of nature," such as a shipwrecked person or the first humans</note>, natural needs are a consequence of his physical constitution. In the man as a citizen, they are a consequence of the social order <note>original: "conſtitution," here referring to the fundamental framework of laws and social structures</note>, without which society could not subsist.

These needs are few in number and grant value only to items of primary necessity. Artificial needs, on the contrary, multiply with—

our habits, and give value to a multitude of products and processed materials <note>original: "matieres travaillées," referring to raw materials that have been manufactured or refined by human labor</note>, which we have placed among the things of secondary necessity.

The value of these things, in proportion to their rarity and their abundance, varies further according to the true or false opinion <note>this highlights an early "subjective theory of value," where the perception of scarcity is as influential as physical supply</note> that we have of that rarity and that abundance.

These values, estimated by comparison, are what we call the **price** of things. From this it follows that, in exchanges, things are reciprocally the price of one another, and that we are all at once, in various respects, sellers and buyers.

It is through the **competition** <term>competition: in this context, the "concurrence" or rivalry between multiple buyers and sellers that prevents any single person from dictating the price</term> of sellers and buyers that prices are regulated. They can only be regulated at **Markets**, and they will vary little there if everyone is permitted to bring what they want and the quantity they want.

Now, the exchanges that take place in Markets are what we call **Commerce**.

It is then that, the number of Merchants not being as large as it could be, the monopoly, which establishes itself upon the ruins of liberty, puts grain up for sale in too large or too small a quantity, according as it is in its interest to make the price fall or rise. However, while it is important that grain always be for sale, because it is always being consumed; it is no less important that it only be put up for sale in the amount that is needed for consumption.

<margin>Distribution of wealth from one rural area to another.</margin>

Nature often presented obstacles which, even after being smoothed away, still caused great expenses for the transport of goods.

A Company creates a monopoly on salt.

Salt, which is very common in our four Monarchies, was, through the freedom of Trade, at a price proportionate to the means of even the least wealthy Citizens; and it was consumed in great quantities, because it is necessary for men, for livestock, and even for the land, for which it is an excellent fertilizer.

There must therefore have been a great profit to be made from a monopoly on salt. A plan was formed, and for this purpose a privileged and exclusive Company was created. It gave the Sovereign a considerable sum, and it granted the Great <note>original: "Grands"; referring to the high-ranking nobility or influential figures at court.</note> who protected it a share of its profits. Those who made up this Company were called *Contractors* <note>original: "Traitans"; these were private financiers who contracted with the Crown to collect taxes or manage state monopolies for a profit.</note>, because they had "treated" <note>In this context, to "treat" means to negotiate a formal contract or treaty.</note> with the King. <margin>How the fineness of coins is determined.</margin>
**W**e have seen that coins are portions of metal upon which public authority has placed an imprint to make known the quantity of gold and silver they contain.

<margin>How much these frauds harm Commerce.</margin>

<margin>Advantage of cultivating the land over the exploitation of mines.</margin>
There comes a time, then, when the exploitation of mines can no longer be carried out profitably. It is not the same for the cultivation of produce <note>The author is likely reflecting the views of the "Physiocrats," an 18th-century group of French economists who believed that agriculture was the only true source of wealth because it is "productive" (it creates new matter), whereas manufacturing and mining were seen as merely "transformative."</note> which is consumed only to be reproduced. Because of the abundance with which these crops are renewed, they multiply with every cycle—both in proportion to the quantity necessary for our consumption and in proportion to the investments <note>French: *avances*. Thus, regardless of the costs involved, the harvest always ensures a profit. It is a source that never runs dry. The more one draws from it, the more it grows. Such is the advantage of cultivating the land over the exploitation of mines.

What would have happened if gold and silver had become as common as iron? These metals would have ceased to be the common measure of values <note>In 18th-century economic theory, the "common measure" refers to the standard by which all goods are priced. If gold were common, it could no longer serve as a stable currency.</note>, and it would no longer have been possible for landowners to receive their income in the cities where they lived. Forced to retreat to their lands, and unable to cultivate them all by themselves, they would have abandoned the greater part of them to settlers <note>French: *colons*. There would be no more cities, and consequently, no more great fortunes. But there would also be no more beggary; and in place of our Monarchies—where misery and depopulation grow continually—we would see a multitude of agricultural cities, which would become more populated every day. How happy we would be if we found mines rich enough to make all our gold and all our silver useless!

<margin>What is meant by the Regulation of Grain.</margin>

## CHAPTER XIV.
### *Attacks on Trade: Maneuvers of the Monopolists.*

<margin>The privilege of conducting a monopoly is purchased.</margin>
**W**e have seen <term>monopoly<note>original: "monopole"; the exclusive control of a commodity or trade, preventing free competition.</note></term> arise from the <term>Regulations<note>original: "Réglemens"; official administrative decrees governing the trade of essential goods.</note></term> made for the policing of <term>grain<note>original: "grains"; the staple cereal crops, primarily wheat, essential for the survival of the population.</note></term>. Since my intention is to reveal the maneuvers of the Monopolists, I would need them to provide me with their own <term>memoirs<note>original: "mémoires"; personal accounts or insider reports.</note></term>. I will limit myself to a few observations.

One could not trade in <term>wheat<note>original: "bleds"; an archaic spelling of "blés," referring generally to wheat and other grains.</note></term> without having obtained permission. But it was not enough to ask for it to obtain it: it was also necessary to have <term>protection<note>original: "protection"; political patronage or influence within the royal administration.</note></term>; and protection was hardly granted except to those who paid for it, or who yielded a share of their <term>profit<note>original: "bénéfice."</note></term>.

The right to conduct a monopoly on grain was thus sold, in a way, to the <term>highest and last bidder<note>original: "plus offrant & dernier enchérisseur"; a standard legal phrase used in public auctions.</note></term>; and often, when one had...

# CHAPTER XV.

## *Attacks on Commerce: Obstacles to the circulation of grain, when the Government wishes to restore to Commerce the liberty it has taken away.*

---

<margin>When the liberty of Commerce has been destroyed, it takes time to restore it.</margin>
The <term>monopolists<note>original: "Monopoleurs"; private individuals or agents who controlled the supply of a commodity to manipulate prices.</note></term> were always creating <term>shortages<note>original: "disette"; a scarcity of food, often local or artificial, that leads to high prices and distress.</note></term> somewhere, or at least high prices, when, in one of our Monarchies, this part of the administration was entrusted to a <term>Minister<note>Likely an allusion to Anne-Robert-Jacques Turgot, who attempted to establish free trade in grain in France in 1774, leading to the "Flour War" riots.</note></term> who restored liberty to Commerce.

But, when the disorder has reached a certain point, a revolution, however wise it may be, is never completed without causing violent shocks; and it is often necessary to take countless precautions to restore order.

In discussing the <term>circulation of grain<note>The logistical and economic process of moving grain from regions of surplus to regions of scarcity to ensure food security and price stability.</note></term>, we have seen that it can only be achieved through a multitude of merchants, spread throughout every region. The liberty restored to the **Grain Trade** was therefore a benefit that could not be enjoyed as soon as it was granted. A single word from the **Monarch** <note>King Louis XVI, who, under the advice of Turgot, signed the edict establishing free trade in grain in September 1774.</note> had been able to annihilate this liberty; a single word could not recreate it, and **high prices** <note>original: "cherté"; a term frequently used in this period to describe the scarcity and resulting high cost of bread which caused public distress.</note> occurred just a few months later.

<margin>Faulty reasoning of those who attribute high prices to liberty.</margin>
"This is what liberty produces." Such was the reasoning of the **People**, and the **People** comprised almost the entire **Nation**. They believed that the high prices were a direct effect of liberty. They refused to see that the **monopoly** could not fall under the first blows struck against it, and that there could not yet be enough **Merchants** to bring grain to its true price.

"But," it was said, "we need bread every day. Now, simply because there is the liberty to bring it to us, is it certain that it will be brought? Do we not run the risk of going without?"

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *Attacks on Trade: The Jealousy of Nations.*

<margin>Assumptions.</margin>
In order to judge what must happen to several jealous Nations, each of which attempts to trade exclusively <note>The author is describing "mercantilism," an economic theory where nations sought to enrich themselves by restricting trade with rivals and maintaining a monopoly over their own markets.</note>, I am transporting the People we have observed to Asia Minor <note>A geographical region comprising most of modern-day Turkey.</note>. I grant them Mysia, Lydia, Bithynia, and still other Provinces, and I create a Kingdom of which Troy shall be the Capital.

But because I wish to observe only the effects of the jealousy of Nations, I assume—in order to set aside every other cause—that this People no longer has, in its customs or its Government, any of the vices for which I have reproached it. It will now be an agricultural Nation. It cultivates the Arts <note>In this context, "Arts" refers to technical skills, crafts, and industrial processes.</note> related to Agriculture; it is beginning to cultivate others; it places more refinement in the comforts of life.

Their goal is to ensure the greatest possible profit.

<margin>Speculations of farmers.</margin>
A Farmer <term>Farmer: The author uses the term *fermier*, which in this era specifically referred to a wealthy entrepreneur who leased large estates from the nobility to run as a commercial business, as opposed to a peasant laborer.</term>, who takes land on lease, estimates its yield based on harvests in average years and on the current price of commodities <note>original: "denrées"</note> in the markets.

This is his first speculation. It is founded upon a conjecture that is more or less plausible, but the outcome remains uncertain. He will make a profit <note>original: "bénéfice"</note> if he harvests as much produce as he anticipated, and if he finds the price he relied upon. In the opposite case, he will suffer losses. Should hail <note>Hail was the most feared natural disaster for French farmers, as a single storm could destroy a year's income. Economic writers often used it to illustrate the fragility of agricultural wealth.</note> strip him of a part of his crops, he will have little produce to sell; and yet he will be forced to sell at a low price if his neighbors have had abundant harvests.

The most common works <note>Refers to everyday manufactured goods or "common wares" intended for the general public.</note>, which are for everyone's use, are those where there are the fewest risks to run. ## CHAPTER XIX.

### *Conclusion of the First Two Parts.*

We have seen how wealth, when Trade enjoys an entire and permanent freedom, spreads everywhere. It flows continually from one Province to another. Agriculture flourishes: the <term>Arts</term> <note>In this context, "Arts" refers to both the fine arts and the "mechanical arts"—what we would today call industry, manufacturing, and skilled crafts.</note> are cultivated even in the smallest hamlets: each Citizen finds <term>ease</term> <note>Original: "l’aisance." # Decorative Endpaper

This page features a full-page illustration of historical **marbled paper**, which was traditionally used as an **endpaper** <note>Endpapers are the sheets of paper pasted to the inside covers of a book to hide the binding construction and provide a decorative transition to the text.</note> in high-quality bound manuscripts. 

The pattern displayed here consists of multiple large, tight spirals, a design frequently called a <term>snail pattern</term> or "curl" pattern. This effect was achieved by floating pigments on a liquid bath—usually thickened with carrageenan moss or gum tragacanth—and "combing" or "swirling" the colors before laying the paper onto the surface to lift the design. 

The palette includes:
*   *Burnt orange*
*   *Ochre yellow*
*   *Charcoal grey* 

These colors are blended against a cream-colored base in a fluid, organic fashion. Such work is characteristic of traditional hand-marbling techniques, where no two sheets are ever exactly identical, reflecting the artisanal nature of the book's physical production.

<summary>This page is a visual decorative element featuring a hand-marbled "snail pattern," serving as an endpaper for the manuscript's binding.</summary>
<keywords>marbled paper, bookbinding, snail pattern, endpaper, decorative arts, 18th-century book production</keywords>
